He had taken me in when Papa died, and I loved him. One month I noticed the women stitching collars got less than the men stitching cuffs, same hours, same skill. I couldn't sleep. If I said nothing, I betrayed them. If I shouted, I betrayed him. So I made a list, sat with him after dinner, and showed him the numbers. He was angry. He said I was ungrateful. I came back the next week, and the next. By Diwali, the pay was the same. Your Devika Mausi still says it was the hardest winter of her life.

qa.a: They would finally be paid the same as the men for the same work, a real difference in their lives even if they never knew who pushed for it.

Mehak, twenty, was secretary of the hostel room committee, and the new list was due on the notice board at five. The ground-floor single rooms were few, and the rule was clear: first to students with medical needs, then by lottery.
At lunch, Sonali, her roommate and closest friend for two years, sat down beside her. "Mehak, just put my name on one. You're on the committee. Nobody will know."
Mehak's chest tightened. Sonali had nursed her through dengue last year. But on the list was Farzana, a first-year who used crutches and couldn't manage the stairs.
Mehak walked around the campus twice, then found Sonali in their room. "I can't skip the lottery for you. Then Farzana doesn't get the room she needs. But I'll help you ask the warden about the second-floor corner room."
Sonali stared at her, hurt. Then she said, slowly, "You'd hate yourself if you did it, wouldn't you?"

qa.q: Who was first in line for the ground-floor rooms?
What was Mehak feeling when Sonali asked for a ground-floor room?
qa.a: Her chest tightened because she felt torn between loyalty to a friend who had nursed her and fairness to students like Farzana.

qa.q: How did Mehak work through the tension instead of choosing carelessly?
qa.a: She took time to think, walked around the campus, then explained her reason honestly to Sonali and offered a fair way to help.

qa.q: How does Sonali's view of Mehak change by the end?
qa.a: Sonali is hurt at first, but then seems to understand that Mehak's fairness is part of who she is.

grounding: It shows a young adult torn between fairness for all and loyalty to her closest friend, who thinks it through and keeps to the fair rule while still helping her friend.

"Bidisha, you're in HR now, na?" Lakshmi Mashi put a sweet in her mouth. "Just put Pintu's CV on top. No interview drama. He's your own cousin."
Bidisha put her tea down. "Mashi, I can forward it. But I can't skip the interview for him."
"Why not? Who will know?"
"I will." Bidisha's cheeks went hot. "There are two hundred people who applied. Some of them have nobody inside. If I push Pintu ahead, I'm cheating them."
"So strangers matter more than family?"
"No!" Bidisha looked at Ma for help. "I love Pintu. I'll help him prepare. I'll do mock interviews with him all weekend. I just won't jump the line."
Ma said quietly, "Didi, she's right. If Pintu gets it fairly, nobody can ever say anything."
Lakshmi Mashi was silent, then sniffed. "Mock interviews, then. Saturday. And feed him properly, he forgets to eat when he's nervous."

qa.q: What did Bidisha offer to do with Pintu all weekend?
What was Bidisha feeling when her cheeks went hot?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and torn, not wanting to hurt her aunt or cousin, but sure that skipping the interview would be unfair to the other applicants.

qa.q: What choice did Bidisha make, and why was it thoughtful rather than careless?
qa.a: She refused to skip the process but offered real help preparing Pintu, keeping fairness to strangers while still showing loyalty to family.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Mashi see Bidisha's refusal at first, and how does it shift?
qa.a: At first she sees it as choosing strangers over family, but Ma's words and the offer of help soften her into accepting the mock interviews.

grounding: It shows a young adult torn between fairness to other applicants and loyalty to family, who works through it by refusing to skip the process but helping her cousin prepare.
